summary: Angel learns from Kirsten herself about her affair with Bishop Timothy Archer. Kirsten confesses that she and Tim are setting up an apartment in the Tenderloin, funded by Tim's Discretionary Fund, with Kirsten serving as his secretary and business manager. The chapter explores the emotional and psychological complexity of the affair through Angel's increasingly frantic and grief-stricken responses. Angel recognizes that Kirsten's psychotic son Bill (schizophrenic, institutionalized at Hoover Pavilion, Stanford) will eventually become a complicating factor. The chapter depicts Angel's oscillation between recognition of the scandal's inevitability and desperate attempts to prevent disaster. Tim's affair with Kirsten is shown as a kind of willing self-destruction, a descent into the 'Other Side' that will eventually claim all three of them. Jeff's emotional devastation at being excluded from his father's discoveries abroad (the Zadokite Documents) drives him toward isolation and, implicitly, toward the suicide that will occur later.

themes.name: The seduction of philosophy over reality
The role of fate versus choice

philosophical_concepts.name: The problem of prophecy (seeing disaster coming but being unable to prevent it)

key_events: Kirsten reveals affair to Angel during shopping trip
Discussion of Bill's schizophrenia and his history of episodes
Angel's recognition that she introduced Kirsten to Tim
Tim's continued focus on Zadokite Documents and theology
Angel and Jeff's confrontation about the affair
Angel's prophecy that disaster will follow
narrative_observations: This chapter demonstrates Dick's mastery of depicting psychological states through fragmented, urgent narration. Angel's increasing panic and substance use (marijuana) reflect her understanding that she has unwittingly set in motion events beyond her control. The chapter includes extended discussions of philosophy, theology, and theory that reflect the Bay Area intellectual culture but also the way that intellectual brilliance can mask moral blindness. The narrator explicitly connects Tim's and Kirsten's affair to the larger deaths of the 1960s-70s era (JFK, RFK, MLK, John Lennon).
